coverage_axes.notes: Independent general dictionaries cover impressive appearance and exceptionally high quality.
The sources identify adjective use and directly attest attributive and predicative frames.
Magnificently and magnificence are attested individually.
No productive specialist or legal sense is required; historical ruler-title, elevated-idea, and lavish senses were checked and excluded from the modern core article.
Sources mark historical/archaic uses and attest the evaluative exclamation and modern high-admiration register.
Cambridge, Oxford, Collins/Dictionary.com, and Etymonline cover current pronunciation and word history.

facts.statement: Magnificent describes someone or something as extremely good, beautiful, impressive, or deserving admiration.
facts.source_detail: Main Cambridge adjective definition and learner examples.

facts.statement: Cambridge gives UK /mæɡˈnɪf.ɪ.sənt/ and a US pronunciation with a reduced third-syllable vowel.
facts.source_detail: UK and US pronunciation panels for the adjective.

facts.statement: Magnificent can mean marked by stately grandeur and lavishness or strikingly beautiful and impressive.
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster adjective senses 2 and 3, including sight, cathedral, and physique examples.
Merriam-Webster adjective sense 5 and performance example.

facts.statement: The epithet the Magnificent is used of former famous rulers who were great in deed or exalted in place.
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster adjective sense 1, labelled as limited to former famous rulers.

facts.statement: Magnificent can mean splendid or impressive in appearance.
Magnificent can mean superb, exceptionally good, or very fine.
facts.source_detail: Collins British and American English quality senses.

facts.statement: Magnificent has a less central elevated or noble sense and an archaic great-in-rank sense.
facts.source_detail: Collins British English senses 3 and 4 with archaic label.

facts.statement: Magnificently is the adverb derived from magnificent.
Magnificent is an adjective used both before a noun and after be or look for things that are extremely attractive, impressive, or deserving praise.
facts.source_detail: Oxford definition, building/job examples, and be/look collocation panel.

facts.statement: Oxford lists /mæɡˈnɪfɪsnt/ for both its British and American learner entries.
facts.source_detail: Oxford pronunciation lines for the adjective.

facts.statement: Magnificent entered late Middle English through Old French from Latin magnificent-, meaning making great and based on magnus, great.
Magnificent is attested as an exclamation expressing enthusiastic admiration by 1704.
facts.source_detail: Etymonline chronology for the exclamatory use.

facts.statement: Magnificent comes through Old French from Latin magnificus, literally doing great deeds, combining magnus with a form related to facere.
facts.source_detail: Etymonline main etymology and morphological analysis.

facts.statement: A lavishly munificent or extravagant sense is recorded but is peripheral to the modern learner core.
Magnificence is the corresponding noun for the quality or state of being magnificent.
facts.source_detail: Dictionary word-family information cross-checked with Merriam-Webster's magnificence entry.

facts.statement: Magnificent is a high-admiration term and can also be used informally in weakened exaggeration.

source_union.canonical_statement: Magnificent has a central adjective sense for visually splendid, grand, beautiful, or impressive people and things.
Magnificent has a central evaluative adjective sense meaning exceptionally good, excellent, or deserving high praise.
Current pronunciations place stress on the second syllable; sources record /ɪ/ or a reduced /ə/ in the third syllable, with /ə/ prominent in American transcription.
source_union.rationale: The article reports the major dictionary transcription difference without claiming an absolute regional split.

source_union.canonical_statement: Magnificent came through French from Latin material combining the idea of great with doing or making.
source_union.rationale: This supports the concise etymology section.

source_union.canonical_statement: Magnificently is the common adverb and magnificence is the common noun in the word family.
source_union.rationale: Both forms have current learner value and appear in word formation.

source_union.canonical_statement: Magnificent can stand alone as an enthusiastic exclamation of admiration.
source_union.rationale: The productive exclamation is included under the general evaluative sense.

source_union.canonical_statement: Historical and elevated uses include former-ruler epithets and noble or exalted rank or ideas.
source_union.rationale: These are historical or peripheral and do not justify a separate modern learner sense.

source_union.canonical_statement: A lavishly munificent or extravagant sense is historically recorded.
source_union.rationale: This low-frequency peripheral use was excluded from the modern core article.

source_union.canonical_statement: Magnificent is strongly admiring and may sound deliberately exaggerated in informal contexts.
source_union.rationale: This register distinction is explicitly taught in sense 2.

claim_units.statement: Magnificent describes a visually splendid or strongly impressive person or thing.

source_supports.support_summary: Cambridge directly gives beautiful and impressive evaluation.
Merriam-Webster directly gives grandeur and striking appearance.
Oxford attests adjective frames with building and appearance examples.

claim_units.statement: Magnificent evaluates a result, performance, job, opportunity, or experience as exceptionally good.

source_supports.support_summary: Cambridge directly gives the extremely good sense.
Collins directly gives superb or very fine.
Oxford attests deserving praise and magnificent job.

claim_units.statement: Magnificent bears second-syllable stress and current dictionaries transcribe the third vowel as /ɪ/ or reduced /ə/.

source_supports.support_summary: Cambridge provides current UK and US audio/transcription panels.
Oxford records the /ɪ/ transcription in both learner varieties.
Dictionary.com explicitly records the US and UK transcription difference.

claim_units.statement: Magnificent entered through French from Latin material meaning making or doing great things.

source_supports.support_summary: Oxford directly supplies French, Latin, and magnus history.
Etymonline supplies the Latin morphological analysis.

claim_units.statement: Magnificently is the productive adverb derived from magnificent.

source_supports.support_summary: Collins explicitly lists magnificently as the derived adverb.

claim_units.statement: Magnificence is the common noun for the quality or state of being magnificent.

source_supports.support_summary: Dictionary and Merriam-Webster word-family information support magnificence.

claim_units.statement: Magnificent can be used alone as an enthusiastic exclamation of approval.

source_supports.support_summary: Etymonline directly records the enthusiastic exclamation.

claim_units.statement: Magnificent is strongly admiring and can sound intentionally exaggerated for a small everyday matter.

source_supports.support_summary: Dictionary.com directly notes high admiration and informal weak exaggeration.
